title: Why lawyers lose focus after interruptions on Mac, and fixes to try in 2026
metaTitle: Lawyers Lose Focus After Interruptions: Mac Fixes for 2026
description: Interruptions pull a lawyer's attention off the brief, and getting back takes effort. Here is why focus breaks on a Mac and the fixes to try today.
secondaryKeywords: how to stay focused at work as a lawyer
intro: Lawyers lose focus after interruptions because part of their attention stays on the task they left. A call, a new email or a chat ping pulls you away, and getting back into the brief takes effort you did not plan for. The fixes below need no new software. You can start with Mac settings you already have, then add a few habits from the research.
tldr: Lawyers lose focus after interruptions because attention stays on the old task. Leroy and Glomb call this attention residue.
Microsoft's 2025 Work Trend Index reports about 275 interruptions a day for knowledge workers, not lawyers specifically.
Set up one Focus on your Mac for drafting time. Allow only the people and apps you choose.
Batch email into set times, and write a short ready-to-resume note before each break.
Follow your employer's rules on client data before any tool reads a screen with matter details.

blocks.text: What losing focus after interruptions costs a lawyer

Interruptions cost a lawyer in three ways. The first is time. Each return to a brief, a contract or a demand letter needs time to rebuild. The second is accuracy. When you come back half-remembering the last clause, the error can sit in the draft until someone else finds it. The third is energy, and it adds up over a long week.

No reliable source puts a number on the minutes a lawyer loses per interruption. Most research on interruptions studies office workers in general. Treat any exact figure you see online with care. Then measure your own week. Write down each interruption for two days, along with what you were doing before it.

The wider picture is harder to look at. The 2026 ABA/CoLAP-Krill study reports that 47% of lawyers screened positive for high burnout. About 27% said they were considering leaving the profession because of mental health, burnout or stress. Burnout here is a self-screen, not a diagnosis. Interruptions are one part of a heavy workload, not the whole cause.

For scale, the Bureau of Labor Statistics put the May 2025 median lawyer wage at $159,670, or $76.76 an hour. That is pay for the work, not a billing rate. If you bill by the hour, lost focus has a real price. The wage figure cannot tell you what that price is.
Why it happens: attention residue and the open task

The best-supported explanation is attention residue. Leroy and Glomb ran four studies on what happens when people are pulled off a task. Their 2018 paper in Organization Science found that anticipating a return to the interrupted task, under time pressure, makes it harder to shift attention to the new one. Part of the mind stays on the old task. Performance on the interrupting task can drop.

This matters for lawyers because deadlines are built into the work. A motion due at five, a client who wants a call back and a phone that keeps lighting up all create time pressure. The study points at the worry about getting back in time, not only at the interruption. That gives you something to plan. You may not control the interruption, but you can plan the return.

items: Deadlines stack. A filing, a hearing and a client call can all land on one afternoon.
Channels multiply. Mail, messages, calendar alerts and phone calls each claim a share of your attention.
Returns are unplanned. When you stop mid-sentence with no note, the next return costs more effort.
Habits pull. Checking email between tasks feels like progress, even when it breaks the task you are on.

blocks.text: Where interruptions come from on a Mac

Microsoft's 2025 Work Trend Index says that during the 9 to 5, employees are interrupted about every 2 minutes by meetings, emails or pings. The report adds up to 275 interruptions a day, including activity outside core hours. The survey covered 31,000 workers in 31 countries. It does not say how the 275 count was measured, and it covers knowledge workers in general, not lawyers.

On a Mac, the usual sources are easy to list. Mail and Outlook show banners. Messages and other chat apps show badges in the Dock. Calendar alerts go off in the middle of drafting. Each one is small. Together they cut the day into pieces. Write down your top three sources before you change anything.
How to stay focused at work as a lawyer: fixes you can start today

None of the fixes below needs an app purchase. They use Mac settings you already have, plus habits from the research. Start with one. Give it a week before you add the next, so you can tell what helped.

items: Set up a Focus for drafting time, with a short allow list.
Schedule the Focus by app, so it starts when Word opens.
Batch email into set check times instead of answering every banner.
Turn off banners for the mail apps you check on a schedule.
Write a ready-to-resume note before each break or call.

blocks.text: Set up a Focus mode for drafting time

Open Apple menu > System Settings > Focus, then click Add Focus. Choose a provided Focus, or pick Custom to name your own. Apple says you can create up to ten custom Focuses. Each Focus can allow certain people and apps through. Under Focus Filters, Mail and Calendar can be customized while the Focus is on.

A Focus can start by time, by location or when an app opens. A Word schedule works well for review days. The Focus turns on when Word opens and turns off when you close it or switch apps. Location schedules need Location Services turned on. Apple also has Intelligent Breakthrough and Silencing, which lets important notifications through. It is always on, and it cannot be turned off if the Reduce Interruptions Focus has been added. Check that before a busy week.
Turn email checks into set times

Kushlev and Dunn asked 124 adults to limit email checks to three times a day during one week. In another week they checked as often as usual. Participants felt less stressed in the limited week. Most found the limit hard to keep, so plan for that. Start with a morning check, a midday check and a late-afternoon check.

In Apple Mail, open Mail > Settings > General and set how often Mail checks for new messages. In Outlook, open Outlook > Settings and review the Mail options. Then open System Settings > Notifications, pick Mail or Microsoft Outlook, and turn off banners. Menu labels can shift between macOS versions, so look for the app name.
Write a ready-to-resume note before each break

Leroy and Glomb tested a brief ready-to-resume step. People reflect on the interrupted work and plan how they will return to it. In their studies, this step reduced attention residue, and performance on the interrupting task did not suffer. The paper reports no effect sizes, so do not expect a fixed gain. Keep the note short. Name the next sentence to write and the open question.

Dictation makes the note faster to write. Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. Typing the note works too. The point is to write it before you leave the task, not to find the perfect words.

blocks.title: Start small
blocks.text: Set one Focus this week. Add email check times next week. Two changes at once make it hard to tell which one helped.
A worked example: a litigator with a motion due Friday

Consider a litigator with a motion due Friday, two client calls and a partner who sends notes at odd hours. Without a plan, the day becomes a string of returns. With a plan, the day has blocks. The table shows one way to set it up. Adjust the times to fit your calendar and your court deadlines.

rows: Draft the motion section with the drafting Focus on
Calls from the client, partner messages
Check email, answer what matters, close Mail
Client call in a fixed slot
Edit and check citations in Word
Write the ready-to-resume note and plan tomorrow
blocks.caption: A sample drafting day with set blocks. Adjust the times to your calendar.

blocks.text: Notice what the plan does not do. It does not promise zero interruptions. It sets the rule for which ones get through and when you look at the rest. If a deadline moves, edit the table, not your whole week. Keep the changes small so the blocks still hold.
Mistakes people make with focus routines

items: Turning on Focus and then checking every banner anyway. The Focus only helps while it is on.
Allowing everyone through. A Focus that lets in all email is not a Focus.
Using one Focus for every task. Drafting and client calls need different rules.
Starting with too many check times. Begin with three, as the study did, and move up only if it works.
Skipping the ready-to-resume note because it feels like extra work. A short note is enough.
Treating notifications as a to-do list. A banner is not a task, so write the task down.

Privacy and client data before you use any tool

blocks.title: Client data comes first
blocks.text: Follow your employer's rules on client and matter data before you let any AI tool read a screen that shows client details. Ask your firm's IT or risk team if you are unsure.

Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Those are product facts from Lazur, not advice about your firm's rules. Many firms limit which tools can see client files, so check before you use voice help on a matter.
Next steps this week

Start with one change today. Set up one Focus for drafting, then run it for a week. Add the email check times after that. If Outlook is your main inbox, read the [Outlook for lawyers guide](/for/lawyers/outlook) before you change any notification settings. When you want voice help on the Mac, you can [download Lazur](/download) and try it with your own screen.

faq.question: Is it normal to lose focus after an interruption?
faq.answer: Yes. Leroy and Glomb's 2018 studies found that anticipating a return to an interrupted task, under time pressure, makes it harder to shift attention to something new. The effect is about how attention works, not about willpower. The fix is a plan for the return.

faq.question: Will a Mac Focus block urgent calls from a partner or court?
faq.answer: A Focus lets through the people and apps you allow. Apple also has Intelligent Breakthrough and Silencing, which passes important notifications and silences the rest. It is always on, and you cannot turn it off if the Reduce Interruptions Focus has been added. Test your settings before a busy week.

faq.question: Can a Focus turn on automatically when I open Word?
faq.answer: Yes. On a Mac, a Focus can turn on when an app opens and turn off when that app closes or you switch away from it. Location schedules need Location Services turned on.

faq.question: How many Focuses can I create on a Mac?
faq.answer: Apple says you can create up to ten custom Focuses. Start from a provided Focus or pick Custom. Many lawyers use one Focus for drafting, one for client calls and one for the end of the day.

faq.question: Is it safe to use Lazur with a screen that shows client details?
faq.answer: Check your employer's rules first. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you and are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Many firms still limit which tools can see client files.

faq.question: Does limiting email checks actually reduce stress?
faq.answer: The Kushlev and Dunn study found that participants felt less stressed in the week they checked email three times a day. It had 124 adults and relied on self-reports. Most people found the limit hard to keep. Treat it as a reason to try, not as proof for your practice.

faq.question: Is there a study on interruptions specifically for lawyers?
faq.answer: Not one this page can cite with confidence. The sources here measure knowledge workers in general or test focus in other settings. Measure your own interruptions for two days and compare the numbers over time.

costs.title: Lost time on every return
costs.text: Each return to work starts with a short rebuild. You reopen the file, find your place and reload the argument. No reliable source gives a number of minutes for lawyers, so measure your own returns for two days before you decide what it costs you.

costs.title: Errors that surface late
costs.text: A missed clause, a wrong date or a citation you meant to check can slip through when attention is split. Nothing public measures how often this happens in legal work. Review your own drafts for the errors you tend to make after a break.

costs.title: Energy across a long week
costs.text: Constant switching is tiring. The 2026 ABA/CoLAP-Krill study found that 47% of lawyers screened positive for high burnout. The study does not tie burnout to interruptions alone. Fewer broken threads is still one lever you control.

costs.title: Time you cannot bill
costs.text: If you bill by the hour, time lost to switching is time you cannot bill. The BLS wage figure of $159,670 is pay, not a billing rate, so it cannot show that cost. Use your firm's own rate and your own log to estimate it.

causes.title: Attention residue after a switch
causes.text: Leroy and Glomb describe attention residue as thinking that stays on the old task after you have moved on. Their four studies, published in 2018, found that this residue makes the new task harder and can lower performance on it. For a lawyer, that means the first ten minutes of the next task can be weaker than they should be.

causes.title: Time pressure on the way back
causes.text: The same studies found that anticipating a return under time pressure makes the switch harder. A lawyer with a deadline already feels that pressure. The worry about getting back in time adds to the cost of the interruption itself.

causes.title: Many channels that all sound urgent
causes.text: Microsoft's 2025 report describes interruptions from meetings, emails and pings during the working day. For knowledge workers, it counts about 275 a day. A lawyer may face a similar mix, with mail, messages, calendar alerts and calls all competing for the same attention.

causes.title: Email checking as a habit
causes.text: In the Kushlev and Dunn study, people who checked email less often felt less stressed. Most of them found the limit hard to keep. That tells you the pull is real. Checking feels productive, but it often breaks the task you are on.

causes.title: No planned stopping point
causes.text: When you stop mid-sentence with no note, the next return takes more effort. This is an inference from the ready-to-resume finding, not a tested claim about lawyers. It is still a practical reason to write a short note before you leave a task.

causes.title: Banners and badges stay on
causes.text: Notification banners and app badges keep pulling at you until you change them. Each one looks small. Over a day, they split your work into pieces that are hard to join back together.

fixes.title: Set a Focus with allowed people and apps
fixes.text: A Focus mutes what you do not want right now and lets through what you do. Choose the people and apps that can reach you during drafting time. Keep the list short, because a long allow list brings the interruptions back.

fixes.title: Schedule the Focus by app
fixes.text: A Focus can switch on when Word opens and switch off when you close it or move to another app. That removes the step of remembering to turn it on. It also ends the Focus with the work, not when you remember to stop.

fixes.title: Batch email into set times
fixes.text: Check email at set times instead of every time a banner appears. The Kushlev and Dunn study tested three checks a day against normal checking. Participants felt less stressed in the limited week. Start with three set times and adjust from there.

fixes.title: Turn off banners for mail apps
fixes.text: Open System Settings > Notifications, pick Mail or Microsoft Outlook, and turn off banners. Keep the app badge if you want a count to check at your set time. Menu labels can shift between macOS versions, so look for the app name.

fixes.title: Write a ready-to-resume note
fixes.text: Before you stop, write the next step and the open question. Leroy and Glomb found that a brief ready-to-resume step reduced attention residue, and performance on the interrupting task did not suffer. The paper reports no effect sizes, so keep your expectations modest.

fixes.title: Dictate the note instead of typing it
fixes.text: Hold fn and speak the note. Lazur dictates clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. Dictation is unlimited on Pro and Power. Typing the note works too. The point is to write it before you leave the task.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Count your interruptions
plan.text: Keep a tally of every interruption for one workday. Note the source, the time and what you were doing before it. The list shows which fix to start with, and it does not require buying anything.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Set up one Focus for drafting
plan.text: Open System Settings, go to Focus, and add a Focus for drafting. Allow only your key contacts and the apps you need. Test it on one real task before you trust it.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Set email check times
plan.text: Pick a morning check, a midday check and a late-afternoon check, or times that suit your calendar. Turn off mail banners between them. Keep the times on a note beside your screen.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Write ready-to-resume notes
plan.text: Before each break or call, write a short note. Name the next step and the open question. Use dictation with fn if typing is slow. Read the note when you come back, before you open the file.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Review and adjust
plan.text: Compare your tally with Day 1. Did the interruptions drop, or did they only move? Keep the rule that worked, drop the one that did not, and check firm rules before you share a screen with client details.
